messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Non-profit Worker
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajan is a 68-year-old South Asian man, divorced, who works part-time for a small nonprofit organization focused on immigrant resettlement services in a mid-sized American city. He came to therapy seven months after being raped by a man he had trusted — a longtime acquaintance who had offered him a ride home after a community fundraising event. What began as a familiar journey through quiet streets ended when the man pulled into an unlit parking structure, locked the doors, and assaulted Rajan with sustained physical force. Throughout the attack, Rajan heard the low mechanical hum of the parking structure's ventilation system, the man's voice issuing low, controlled instructions, and the sound of his own breathing becoming ragged and then, at some point, almost silent. He did not fight back in the way he had always imagined he would. He went somewhere else in his mind. It was this — the stillness of his own body — that would haunt him most in the months that followed.

In the weeks after the assault, Rajan told no one. He returned to his apartment, which he had lived in alone since his divorce several years earlier, and tried to resume his routines. But the apartment, which had once felt like a refuge, had become something else. He found himself unable to sit in any chair that did not face the door, and he began positioning himself with his back pressed against the wall whenever he sat down — at home, in the office breakroom, at the small community meetings his nonprofit organized for newly arrived families. At work, where he helps coordinate housing placements and legal referrals, he began arriving early specifically to secure a seat against the back wall before others arrived. His colleagues noticed but said nothing at first.

Sleep became shallow and vigilant. He lay awake cataloguing sounds — footsteps in the hallway outside his door, the elevator mechanism, a neighbor's key in a lock — certain each time that someone was entering his home. Unexpected loud sounds, a car backfiring outside his office window or a door slamming in the resettlement center, sent a physical jolt through him that he could not suppress or explain to those nearby. Being touched without warning had become unbearable; during a routine moment when a colleague placed a hand briefly on his shoulder to get his attention, Rajan recoiled so sharply that the room fell quiet.

The memories themselves did not arrive as coherent narrative. Instead, they came in fragments — and when they did, Rajan heard things: the ventilation hum, the man's voice, the specific quality of his own altered breathing. He also felt, in his lower abdomen and pelvis, a dull and then sharp pain that had no current physical source his doctor could identify. When asked in the intake session to describe what had happened, he sat for a long time and then said quietly that he knew everything that had occurred but that the words were simply not available to him — as though language itself had been revoked for this particular knowledge.

Over the months, Rajan had come to believe, with a certainty that felt irrefutable, that his response during and after the assault proved he was fundamentally incapable of managing difficulty — that other men, better men, would have acted differently, recovered faster, spoken sooner. He had come to feel that the emotions he once recognized in himself — warmth toward the families he helped resettle, pleasure in small rituals, connection to his adult children with whom he had been slowly rebuilding a relationship after the divorce — were no longer genuinely accessible to him. What frightened him most, sitting in the intake room, was the possibility that this was permanent. He described himself, carefully and without self-pity, as someone who now stood outside ordinary human life looking in, unable to find the door back.

He had begun hurting himself — pressing his forearm against a hot surface, or digging his nails into his palm — not out of a wish to die, he was clear about that, but because the physical sensation briefly interrupted something internal that had become otherwise unmanageable. It was his youngest daughter, visiting unexpectedly and noticing the marks on his arm, who finally insisted he speak to someone. He came to therapy, he said, because he did not want her to watch him disappear.
